title: When Does Adaptation Win? Scaling Laws for Meta-Learning in Quantum Control
claim: Meta-train a controller on a simulated ensemble of noisy devices, then adapt it with a few gradient steps on each real device.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, dashed meta-training box, saturation-curve inset
description: A three-panel horizontal workflow. Panel (a), "Task ensemble", shows a 3x3 grid of transmon qubits drawn as circles colored by noise rate Γ with a viridis colorbar from low to high. Below it are the distribution ξ ~ P(ξ) and the heterogeneity variance σ²_τ. Panel (b), "Simulate — meta-train on simulator", sits inside a dashed purple box. A differentiable Lindblad simulator box and a FOMAML outer-loop box are joined by arrows carrying ∇L and θ. An arrow labeled "sample" runs from (a) into this box. Panel (c), "Deploy — per-device adaptation", shows one device feeding ξ into a K-gradient-steps box. That box takes θ0 from (b) and outputs θ_K(ξ) and a red control pulse waveform. Below it, a red exponential saturation curve G_K marks A∞ and K*. Gray italic notes along the bottom give the gradient method for each panel. The eye goes first to the central boxes and arrows.
caption: Simulate-then-deploy workflow for meta-learned quantum control. (a) A heterogeneous processor of transmons with noise rates $\xi = (\Gamma_{\mathrm{deph}}, \Gamma_{\mathrm{relax}}) \sim \mathcal{P}(\xi)$; heterogeneity is summarized by $\sigma_\tau^{2} = \mathrm{Var}(\Gamma_{\mathrm{deph}}) + \mathrm{Var}(\Gamma_{\mathrm{rel}})$. (b) A differentiable Lindblad simulator ($\dot{\rho} = \mathcal{L}_{\xi}[\rho]$), with noise model fit from device characterization, is meta-trained via first-order model-agnostic meta-learning (FOMAML) on tasks $\{\xi_i\} \sim \mathcal{P}$ to yield initialization $\theta_0$. $\eta_0$ and $g_{meta}$ are the outer loop learning rate and meta-gradient. (c) At deployment, relaxation and dephasing times ($T_1$ and $T_2$) via Rabi and Ramsey characterization supplies $\xi$; $K$ gradient steps produce $\theta_K(\xi)$ parameterizing the emitted control pulse $u(t;\theta_K)$. The saturation curve $G_K = A_{\infty}(1 - e^{-\beta K})$ (inset) characterizes the adaptation gain, with $K^{*}$ marking diminishing returns.
abstract: Quantum hardware suffers from intrinsic device heterogeneity and environmental drift, forcing practitioners to choose between suboptimal non-adaptive controllers or costly per-device recalibration. We derive a scaling law lower bound for meta-learning showing that the adaptation gain (expected fidelity improvement from task-specific gradient steps) saturates exponentially with gradient steps and scales linearly with task variance, providing a quantitative criterion for when adaptation justifies its overhead. Validation on quantum gate calibration shows negligible benefits for low-variance tasks but >40% fidelity gains on two-qubit gates under extreme out-of-distribution conditions (10$\times$ the training noise), with implications for reducing per-device calibration time on cloud quantum processors. Further validation on classical linear-quadratic control confirms these laws emerge from general optimization geometry rather than quantum-specific physics. We further introduce a few-shot pre-adaptation protocol that estimates the optimal adaptation budget from $N{=}3$-5 probe steps within 3-19% relative error across out-of-distribution regimes.
